headline: SW Ledge slack at 9:40: stripers deep, bonito still a rip away
subhead: The current's building into the new moon, the bass are holding on structure after dark, and the bonito push is knocking on Block Island's door but hasn't walked in yet.
body_markdown:
Slack tide hit SW Ledge at 9:40 this morning, and for about twenty minutes the whole rip went flat calm before the ebb grabbed hold again — that's the window I want my clients rigged and ready in, because the first hard push of moving water after slack is when the bass show themselves on the ledge in 35 to 45 feet. This week that window produced, but it wasn't a bell-ringer. We picked at fish rather than loaded the box.

Here's where things stand heading into the August 12 new moon: the tidal range is building fast, and you can feel it in how much harder the ledge is pulling on both the last hour of the ebb and the first hour of the flood. We flagged this pattern last week — said the deep/night bite on stripers would hold until either a cooling trend or the new moon tides stirred things up — and that's exactly what's playing out. The bass haven't left, they've just gone conservative. Best fish this week came off SW Ledge after dark, drifting live eels on 3-ounce egg sinkers along the west face where the rip stacks bait against the rock in 30 to 40 feet on the last two hours of the outgoing. A couple of fish pushing 30 pounds came off that drift Tuesday night, along with a scattering of schoolies that told me there's still plenty of biomass sitting on that structure, just not stacked tight the way it gets once the current really starts ripping through mid-month.

Now the part I don't sugarcoat: if you're fishing Block Island itself for stripers right now, particularly around Southeast Light and the deeper structure off the south side, be smart about your fight times. The brown sharks have moved into that zone hard this summer, and the mortality rate on released bass that get worked over before they hit the boat is ugly — we're talking somewhere near 90 percent on fish that get chased down after release. If you're keeping your legal fish, fine, but if you're catch-and-release fishing around Block right now, get them up fast, handle them quick, and consider working shallower water off Clay Head or up toward North Light where the sharks haven't set up shop yet. It's not the kind of thing that shows up in a tide table, but it should factor into where you point the bow.

Fluke have been a grind. We're marking bait on the meter around the mussel beds off Sandy Point and in the deeper cuts off the west side, but the drift has been inconsistent — some days you hit six or eight keepers to 4 pounds on white Gulp Swimming Mullets tipped with squid strips on 3/4-ounce bucktails, other days you burn three hours for two fish. The warm surface water is pushing the better fluke down into 25 to 35 feet where the temperature break holds, so I've been slowing the drift with a sea anchor to keep bait in the strike zone longer instead of covering ground fast. Sea bass have been the more reliable play — the rock piles east of the Ledge and the rubble bottom off Galilee's outer breakwater are holding a steady grade of 14 to 17-inch fish on Asian jigs tipped with squid, especially the first two hours of the incoming when the current isn't ripping too hard to hold bottom.

And then there's the fish everyone's asking about at the dock every single morning: bonito. They are not here yet. I want to be straight about that because I've had three separate charters ask me to run out looking for them this week, and we came up empty every time. What I can tell you is the push through Watch Hill and Sakonnet is real and it's already bled into Buzzards Bay, which is the leading edge of what should be this season's first wave. We called this exact trigger last week too — said the new moon's building current would be what finally pushes bait hard enough through the rips to bring albies and bonito into range at Montauk, Block Island, and the Vineyard corridor. With the moon going new on the 12th and the tidal range already ramping at SW Ledge, I expect the first confirmed fish off Block — likely working the rip off North Light or the current seam running south off Sandy Point — sometime in the next four to seven days. That's not a guess pulled from nowhere; that's the same current mechanics that bring bait piling through those rips every August, just running a few days behind the Rhode Island mainland side this year.

If I had one trip to make this week, I'd fish the last hour of the outgoing at SW Ledge for stripers after dark, then swing out to North Light at first light and idle the rip with a bucktail rigged and ready in case a bonito shows on the surface. No promises on the albie — but the pieces are lining up, and I'd rather be out there when it happens than reading about it at the dock the next morning.
